---
title: "Part 4 — When it breaks"
---

## The universal first move

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Something's wrong with git. Here's the whole error: [paste everything].
> What's the state of my repository and what should I do?
:::

Paste the **entire** message, hints included. Git's hints usually contain the
answer, and students habitually paste only the first red line.

Before anything else, two harmless commands that tell you where you are:

```bash
git status
git log --oneline --graph -10
```

Nothing in this world is lost as long as you committed it. Git's default
behaviour is to refuse to destroy work; almost every alarming message is git
*protecting* you.

## The five errors you will actually meet

All five outputs below are real, captured from the worked example.

### 1. Rejected push

``` text
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally.
```

**What it means** — a teammate pushed; you would be overwriting them.

**Fix** — `git pull`, resolve anything that conflicts, then `git push`.

**Never** — `git push --force`. That deletes your teammate's commits from
GitHub.

### 2. Need to specify how to reconcile

``` text
fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.
```

**What it means** — you and GitHub both have new commits, and git has not been
told whether to merge or rebase. Not your fault: a missing setting.

**Fix** — the Part 0 line you skipped:

```bash
git config --global pull.rebase false
git pull
```

### 3. Merge conflict

``` text
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in report.qmd
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

**What it means** — the same lines changed on both sides. Working as designed.

**Fix** — see [Part 3](03-collaborate.qmd). Or escape with `git merge --abort`, which puts
everything back untouched.

### 3b. Your pull request says CONFLICTING

``` text
mergeable        : CONFLICTING
mergeStateStatus : DIRTY
```

**What it means** — your branch was fine when you made it, but `main` moved on
underneath you and touched the same lines. Your push was never rejected, so
this is the first you hear of it.

**Fix** — bring `main` into your branch, not the other way round:

```bash
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
# resolve, check it renders, then:
git push
```

The PR updates itself. Full walkthrough in [Part 3½](03b-pr-conflict.qmd).

**Watch out** — in this conflict the other side is work your group has already
reviewed and merged. Default to keeping it and adding yours.

### 4. Author identity unknown

``` text
*** Please tell me who you are.
Run
  git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
  git config --global user.name "Your Name"
fatal: empty ident name (for <>) not allowed
```

**What it means** — git will not stamp a commit with nobody's name.

**Fix** — run the two lines it gives you. Use the email your GitHub account
uses, or GitHub will not link the commits to you.

### 5. You committed something huge or secret

Not one error message but several — a push that hangs for minutes, or GitHub
refusing a file over 100 MB.

**Fix** — if you have **not pushed yet**, this is easy:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> I accidentally committed `data/huge_export.csv` in my last commit and haven't
> pushed. Undo that commit, keep my other changes, and add the file to
> .gitignore.
:::

**If you have already pushed a secret**, the situation is different and you
should tell your instructor. Rewriting shared history is disruptive, and — the
important part — **assume the secret is already compromised.** Revoke the API
key, change the password. Removing it from the repository does not un-publish
it.

## Prompt cheat-sheet

Say these instead of learning commands.

### Every day

| What you want | Say |
|---|---|
| Start work | *"Pull the latest changes and tell me what my teammates changed."* |
| Save progress | *"Commit my work with a message explaining why I made this change."* |
| Publish it | *"Push this to GitHub."* |
| Start a task | *"Make a branch for adding the age-adjusted model."* |
| Submit it | *"Push this branch and open a pull request explaining what and why."* |
| After it's merged | *"My PR was merged — update my main and delete the old branch."* |

### Finding out what is going on

| What you want | Say |
|---|---|
| Where am I? | *"What branch am I on, and is anything uncommitted?"* |
| What changed? | *"Show me what I've changed since my last commit."* |
| Who did this? | *"Who last changed the model in R/03-model.R, and what was the message?"* |
| Recent history | *"Summarise what the group has done in the last week."* |
| Am I behind? | *"Am I behind GitHub? What would I get if I pulled?"* |

### Fixing things

| What you want | Say |
|---|---|
| Undo uncommitted mess | *"Throw away my uncommitted changes to R/02-describe.R."* |
| Undo last commit, keep work | *"Undo my last commit but keep the changes in my files."* |
| Undo a merged contribution | *"Revert the commit that added the sex-stratified table."* |
| Go back and look | *"Show me report.qmd as it was three commits ago."* |
| Wrong branch | *"I did this work on main by mistake. Move it to a new branch."* |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two prompts to be careful with

*"Throw away my changes"* and *"undo my last commit"* can destroy work that
was never committed, which is the one kind git cannot recover.

Before agreeing to anything that discards work, ask: **"what exactly will be
lost?"** A good answer names files. If you are unsure, commit first — a commit
you do not want is easy to discard later; uncommitted work you deleted is gone.
:::

## What not to delegate

| Delegate freely | Decide yourself |
|---|---|
| Writing commit messages | Whether your code is correct |
| `add`/`commit`/`push`/`pull`/branches | Which version of a conflict is right |
| Writing `.gitignore` | Whether a data file may be published at all |
| Opening pull requests | Whether a teammate's PR should be merged |
| Explaining an error | Whether to force-push (answer: no) |

The pattern: **anything reversible and mechanical, delegate. Anything about
meaning or about publishing, own.**
